questions.lead_in: What vaccination would be most appropriate?

questions.question: List the conditions and circumstances in which meningococcal serogroup B vaccine is indicated or may be considered.
questions.question_raw: Conditions indicated in – complement deficiency (eculizumab), asplenic, laboratory workers, during menB outbreak, circumstances when could be considered (ie/ outbreak…)

parts.text: List the conditions and circumstances in which meningococcal B vaccine is indicated or may be considered, including complement deficiency or eculizumab use, asplenia, laboratory workers, and serogroup B outbreaks.

parts_raw.text: Conditions indicated in – complement deficiency (eculizumab), asplenic, laboratory workers, during menB outbreak, circumstances when could be considered (ie/ outbreak…)

questions.model_answer:
Recommended (high risk of invasive meningococcal disease):
(1) Persistent complement component deficiency (C3, C5-C9, properdin, factor D, factor H) or treatment with a complement inhibitor (eculizumab, ravulizumab).
(2) Anatomic or functional asplenia, including sickle cell disease.
(3) Laboratory or industrial workers routinely exposed to Neisseria meningitidis isolates.
(4) Close contacts of a case of serogroup B invasive meningococcal disease (as adjunct to chemoprophylaxis), and persons in a defined serogroup B outbreak or hyperendemic setting.
May be considered: travellers to areas with serogroup B outbreaks, adolescents and young adults (including post-secondary students in residence) after shared clinical decision making, and recipients of hematopoietic stem cell transplant or those with HIV where local guidance supports it.
questions.beyond_mandell: NACI meningococcal statement and ACIP MenB recommendations (shared clinical decision making for adolescents 16-23 years).

questions.question: An 18-year-old woman is seen in the infectious diseases clinic 2 weeks after a motor vehicle accident that required splenectomy.
questions.question_raw: PM Q19. 18 year old female 2 weeks post MVA resultant splenectomy

parts.text: What three recommendations (other than vaccines) would you make or discuss with her at the ID appointment?
What four vaccines would you give in the context of splenectomy?

parts_raw.text: a) What 3 recommendations (outside of vaccines) would you make/discuss with her at the ID appointment?
b) What 4 vaccines would you give in the context of splenectomy?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Educate her on the lifelong risk of overwhelming postsplenectomy sepsis and to seek immediate medical attention with fever/chills, communicating her asplenic status; carry a Medic-Alert bracelet (especially for travel). (2) Provide home-supply empirical self-administered antibiotics (e.g. amoxicillin-clavulanate, cefuroxime, or an extended-spectrum fluoroquinolone) to take at onset of fever while proceeding urgently to care; re-prescribe annually. (3) Advise travel precautions - malaria/babesiosis vector avoidance and malaria chemoprophylaxis when travelling to endemic areas. b) (1) Pneumococcal (PCV13 followed >=8 wk later by PPSV23); (2) Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), one dose; (3) Meningococcal - quadrivalent MenACYW plus serogroup B (MenB); (4) Annual seasonal influenza.

cohort_answer.text:
Recommendations: Medical alert bracelet; Abx ppx 2 years post splenectomy; Seek medical attention when febrile; Malaria ppx; Vaccinate household members.
Vaccines: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, polysaccharide pneumococcal vaccine, quad meningococcal vaccine, men B, HiB, influenza

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Pneumococcal conjugate (PCV13/PCV15/PCV20); (2) Pneumococcal polysaccharide PPSV23 (>=8 wk after conjugate); (3) Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib); (4) Quadrivalent conjugate meningococcal MenACYW; (5) Meningococcal serogroup B (MenB); (6) Annual influenza; (7) Hepatitis B; (8) COVID-19 (with Hepatitis A and typhoid where indicated) - plus all routine immunizations. b) (1) MMR (measles-mumps-rubella); (2) Varicella - both live attenuated vaccines whose response is blunted by passively transferred IVIG antibody, so give >=2 weeks before or defer several months after IVIG.
questions.beyond_mandell: The specific NACI eight-vaccine asplenia list (COVID-19, hepatitis A/B, typhoid) and the IVIG-live-vaccine deferral interval are from NACI/PHAC Canadian Immunization Guide; Mandell (CDC/ACIP-based) covers the pneumococcal, Hib, meningococcal, and influenza components.

cohort_answer.text: 8 vaccines: PPV23, PCV13, Hib, Quadrivalent conjugated meningococcal, Meningococcal B, Influenza vaccine, Hepatitis A (for people with repeated transfusions), Hepatitis B (as above), Salmonella typhi vaccine if indicated. Vaccines to delay with IVIG: MMR and varicella

questions.question_raw: Man with E coli meningitis with rapidly expanding perianal rash.

parts.text: What is the likely cause?
Give two infectious risk factors for this.
Give two non-infectious risk factors for this.
Name three diagnostic tests.
What are the precautions?

parts_raw.text: What is the likely cause?
Two infectious risk factors for this.
Two non-infectious risk factors for this.
3 Diagnostic tests (name 3).
What are the precautions.

questions.model_answer: a) Disseminated strongyloidiasis (Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfection) — enteric gram-negative bacteremia/meningitis from larval gut translocation, with a rapidly migrating perianal serpiginous rash (larva currens). b) (1) HTLV-1 infection. (2) HIV. c) (1) Corticosteroid therapy / immunosuppression. (2) Solid-organ transplant, anti-TNF agents, hematologic malignancy or hypogammaglobulinemia (any two). d) (1) Serology (Strongyloides IgG ELISA). (2) Stool microscopy for larvae (serial O&P; agar plate culture). (3) Examination of sputum/BAL, CSF, or urine for filariform larvae. e) Standard precautions; add contact precautions given larvae in stool/secretions and potential autoinfection.
questions.beyond_mandell: Strongyloides hyperinfection is covered in the Strongyloides chapter, not Mandell ch. 93.

cohort_answer.text: Likely cause: Disseminated Strongyloides. Infectious risk factors: HTLV, HIV-1. Non-infectious risk factors: SOT, anti-TNF drugs, hypogammaglobulinemia, high dose steroids, haematological malignancy. Diagnostic tests: Serology; Stool for O&P (larvae); CSF, urine, blood O&P; BAL for larvae; Agar plate culture. Precautions: Contact precautions because disseminated strongy

questions.model_answer: a) All given >=14 days before elective splenectomy: (1) PCV13 conjugate pneumococcal; (2) PPSV23 polysaccharide pneumococcal, >=8 wk after PCV13; (3) Hib, one dose; (4) Quadrivalent MenACYW (two doses >=8-12 wk apart, MenACYW-D >=4 wk after PCV13); (5) MenB (two/three-dose series, licensed ages 10-25 yr); (6) Annual seasonal influenza. b) (1) Antibiotic prophylaxis / patient-held empirical antibiotics at fever onset with immediate presentation; (2) patient education plus Medic-Alert identification and travel/vector precautions (malaria prophylaxis). c) Capnocytophaga canimorsus. d) Babesia microti (babesiosis).

cohort_answer.text: Vaccines (ideally at least 2 weeks, ideally 10-12 weeks prior to splenectomy): PCV-13 anytime from now; PPV-23 8 weeks after PCV-13; Men B-4C now and second dose 4-8 weeks later; Men ACYW-135 now and second dose 8 weeks later; Haemophilus Type B (regardless of vaccination history); Annual influenza vaccination; all other routine immunizations (HepB, HPV). Other prevention: Daily antimicrobial prophylaxis (beta lactam) for at least 2 years post-splenectomy (adults 1 year), abortive/pill-in-pocket beta lactams, patient/family education, malaria prophylaxis if traveling. Dog bite pathogen: Capnocytophaga canimorsus. New England tick bite pathogen: Babesia microti

questions.question: Discuss functional asplenia.
questions.question_raw: Functional asplenia

parts.text: Name the immunologic deficits secondary to asplenia/hyposplenia.
Name four causes of asplenia.
Name two parasites that may cause severe infection in asplenic patients.

parts_raw.text: Name immunologic deficits secondary to asplenia/hyposplenia
Name 4 causes of asplenia
Name two parasites that may cause severe infection in asplenic patients

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Decreased clearance of unopsonized/circulating bacteria (depleted red pulp macrophages); (2) impaired opsonization and phagocytosis with decreased IgG2 and IgM antibody to polysaccharide/carbohydrate antigens (depleted marginal zone macrophages and germinal-centre B cells); (3) decreased clearance of parasite-infected erythrocytes; (4) dysregulated innate immunity - reduced Toll-like receptor and macrophage scavenger function, decreased B-cell activation, increased TNF. b) (1) Surgical splenectomy for trauma; (2) splenectomy for immune cytopenia (e.g. ITP); (3) splenic infarction/atrophy in sickle cell anemia (congenital hemoglobinopathy); (4) functional hyposplenism from celiac disease, GVHD, or HIV/AIDS. c) (1) Babesia (B. microti); (2) Plasmodium (malaria).

cohort_answer.text: Immunologic deficits: filtration/clearance deficit, adaptive immunity deficit, generation of IgM/IgG to polysaccharides (T cell independent), innate immunity (marginal zone macrophage scavengers). Causes: Congenital asplenia (cyanotic congenital HD), Acquired traumatic (MVC), Acquired infarction (sickle cell disease), Acquired planned surgical resection (ITP), acquired functional hyposplenia (GVHD/HIV/Celiac/SLE). Parasites: Babesia spp., Malaria (bacteria: HiB, S. pneumo, N. meningitidis, C. canimorsus, Salmonella, Bordetella)

questions.model_answer:
a) Four causes of functional hyposplenism: (1) Sickle cell anemia. (2) Graft-versus-host disease after bone marrow/stem cell transplantation. (3) Celiac disease. (4) HIV/AIDS (advanced disease). [Others accepted: alcoholic liver disease, inflammatory bowel disease, primary amyloidosis, SLE.]
b) Two parasitic diseases more severe in asplenia: (1) Babesiosis (Babesia microti) - high-grade parasitemia with significant hemolysis. (2) Malaria (Plasmodium falciparum) - higher parasitemia, more circulating mature forms, increased severity/death and cerebral malaria.

questions.question: A 14-year-old who immigrated from the Philippines one year ago underwent splenectomy 2 weeks ago after a motor vehicle accident. Other than immunizations, what four things should you discuss at this meeting?
questions.question_raw: 14 year old from Philippines immigrated 1 year ago. Splenectomy 2 weeks ago after car accident.

parts.text: Other than immunizations, what four things should you discuss at this meeting?

parts_raw.text: Other than immunizations, what 4 things should you discuss at this meeting?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Antibiotic prophylaxis - daily oral penicillin VK or amoxicillin, particularly in the first years and after any prior sepsis. (2) Patient-held emergency ("standby") antibiotics - self-administer high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate/cefuroxime/fluoroquinolone at the first sign of fever and proceed immediately to an emergency facility; represcribe annually. (3) Education on overwhelming sepsis risk plus a Medic-Alert bracelet and a warning flagged in the medical record - seek urgent care for any fever/chills. (4) Travel/vector precautions - given origin from a malaria- and Babesia-relevant setting, malaria chemoprophylaxis when travelling to endemic areas, insect/tick-bite avoidance, and avoidance of dog bites/scratches (Capnocytophaga canimorsus).

cohort_answer.text: 1. Antibiotic ppx - ideally lifelong amoxicillin 250mg PO BID. 2. Emergency antibiotic supply - present to hospital at first fever/infection sign, consider pill-in-pocket amoxclav. 3. Travel precautions - malaria ppx if travelling to endemic regions, avoid mosquito/tick bites. 4. Animal bites - abx ppx needed for dog bite (C. canimorsus). 5. Other - med alert card or bracelet.

questions.question: A splenectomized 26-year-old man: should you give the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, the polysaccharide vaccine, or both? Explain.
questions.question_raw: Splenectomized 26 year old man. Should you give the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, the polysaccharide vaccine, or both? Explain.

parts.text: Should you give conjugate, polysaccharide, or both? Explain.

parts_raw.text: Should you give conjugate, polysaccharide, or both? Explain

questions.model_answer: a) Give both. In a previously unimmunized asplenic adult, administer the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) first, followed at least 8 weeks later by the polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23). The conjugate vaccine overcomes the splenic dependence of the antipolysaccharide response (T-cell-dependent, better magnitude/durability and immune memory), while PPSV23 is then added to broaden serotype coverage. Revaccinate with PPSV23 once, 5 years after the first PPSV23 dose (for adults up to age 65).

questions.question: A patient is going for splenectomy for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Using the listed vaccines (meningococcal C conjugate, tetravalent polysaccharide, 7-valent conjugate, 23-valent polysaccharide, influenza, typhoid, Haemophilus influenzae type b, MMR), each of which may be used never, once, or more than once, construct a vaccine schedule for before the operation and for one year after.
questions.question_raw: You have a patient who is going for splenectomy for TTP. Make a vaccine schedule with the list of vaccines (menC conjugate, tetravalent polysaccharide, 7-valent conjugate, 23 valent polysaccharide, influenza, typhoid vaccine, HiB, MMR). You can use each vaccine never, once, or more than once. Make the schedule for before the operation and for 1 year after.

parts.text: Make a vaccine schedule before the operation and for one year after.

parts_raw.text: Make a vaccine schedule before the operation and for 1 year after

questions.model_answer:
a) Pre-op (elective splenectomy, all given at least 14 days before operation): pneumococcal conjugate (PCV13) x1; Hib conjugate x1 (even if previously immunized); quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate (MenACYW) x1; MenB series started; influenza vaccine (in season). Do NOT use PCV7 (superseded), tetravalent polysaccharide meningococcal (use conjugate), MMR (live, not indicated for asplenia per se), or typhoid (only if travelling to endemic areas).
After operation (through 1 year): PPSV23 x1 given >=8 weeks after PCV13; MenACYW 2nd dose >=3 months after the first (unimmunized adult) then revaccinate q5yr; complete the MenB series; annual influenza vaccine. Typhoid only if travel to an endemic area.
(Each vaccine used: PCV7 - never; PCV13 - once; PPSV23 - once, later revaccinate at 5 yr; Hib - once; MenACYW conjugate - two doses; MenB - two/three-dose series; tetravalent polysaccharide - never [conjugate preferred]; influenza - annually; MMR - never; typhoid - only if travelling.)
questions.beyond_mandell: Current Canadian NACI practice differs from the older ACIP schedule in the chapter: Pneu-C-20 as a single dose (no PPSV23 needed if a 20-valent conjugate is used), routine MenB, and meningococcal boosters q5yr - use NACI for a Canadian exam answer.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort schedule uses newer Canadian NACI products (Pneu-C-20, routine MenB, revised booster intervals) whereas the chapter reflects the older US ACIP PCV13-then-PPSV23 approach; both prioritize the encapsulated-organism vaccines pre-op with post-op completion.

cohort_answer.text: 2 weeks pre-op (or 2 weeks post-op if emergent): Pneu-C-20 (single dose) OR PCV13/15; HiB (regardless of prior vaccination); Men-C-ACYW; Men-B. 8-10 weeks post initial vaccines: Pneu-P-23 (only if PCV13/15); Men-C-ACYW 2nd dose; Men-B 2nd dose. 1 year after: ACYW q5years and MenB 1 year after completion of primary series and q2-3years thereafter; annual influenza + COVID; typhoid vaccine if travel to endemic areas.

questions.question: A 15-year-old who had a splenectomy for immune thrombocytopenic purpura.
questions.question_raw: 15 year old who had splenectomy for ITP

parts.text: What three vaccines should he have according to NACI guidelines?
What two things will you suggest to further prevent infection?

parts_raw.text: A) What 3 vaccines should he have according to NACI guidelines?
B) What 2 things will you suggest to further prevent infection?

questions.model_answer:
a) Three vaccines against encapsulated organisms: (1) Pneumococcal vaccine (conjugate PCV followed by polysaccharide PPSV23). (2) Meningococcal vaccine (quadrivalent MenACYW; plus MenB in this age group). (3) Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) conjugate. [Annual influenza vaccine is also recommended.]
b) Two further prevention measures: (1) Antibiotic prophylaxis - daily oral penicillin/amoxicillin, plus a supply of patient-held emergency antibiotics for fever. (2) Patient education with a Medic-Alert bracelet and counselling on travel/vector avoidance (malaria chemoprophylaxis and tick avoidance for Babesia when travelling to endemic regions).

questions.model_answer: a) Clostridium septicum (non-traumatic gas gangrene/hemorrhagic bullae in neutropenic malignancy, associated with GI/colorectal lesions). b) Capnocytophaga canimorsus - splenectomy is a strong risk factor for this dog-bite/scratch pathogen. c) Aeromonas hydrophila (fresh-water exposure necrotizing soft-tissue infection). d) Giardia duodenalis (lamblia) - the classic cause of chronic diarrhea in CVID.
